method: Read every assigned target and context body in full from the preserved HTML, then checked the corresponding XML date attributes, source authority, exclusions/apparatus, scholarly siblings, footnotes and bibliography. Compared Darwin targets backward against Henslow contexts and the earlier Darwin outgoing sequence, retaining only source-specific scoped relations and explicit negative holds. HTML figure references were checked; three referenced assets were unavailable locally for visual inspection.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 18 April 1835
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s April letter is an extensive geological report after crossing the Cordilleras. It argues from stratification, fossils, silicified trees and mineral veins for the history of the Andes, marks the limits of his evidence, sends red-snow observations and viviparous lizards for possible expert examination, and specifies seeds, wild potatoes, notebooks and a coming cargo. Its authorial assertions and requests are not responses to any surviving Henslow body in this assignment.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 12 [August] 1835
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin calls this his last letter from the American shore, reports the Conway specimen boxes, revises his geological account of the Andes after travel to Copiapó, discusses secondary versus Tertiary analogies, and asks Henslow to send one more letter to the Cape of Good Hope. The body says a home box with books and a Henslow letter is expected but not yet received; that future item cannot be activated as a prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow [28–9] January 1836
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s final pre-return letter describes the anticipated return, Australian travel and colonial economy, the Galapagos flora, birds and volcanic geology, Tahiti and New Zealand, and the remaining route to England. He says no letter has arrived and treats Henslow’s future handwriting as something still hoped for, so this source supplies no incoming prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow 9 July 1836
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Henslow to take preparatory steps for his election to the Geological Society and reports homesickness, St Helena geology, the remaining route and missed letters chasing the ship. The request for a Cambridge visit and later reunion is prospective; no earlier Henslow letter is identified as its source.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow 6 October [1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: After reaching Shrewsbury, Darwin asks Henslow for an immediate line about whether he is at Cambridge and for advice on handling and describing geological specimens. He is confused about where to go and wants to visit Cambridge before returning to London; the Thursday morning line is an internal dated addition, not an incoming response.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow [30–1 October 1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin reports bringing Galapagos plants from the Beagle, plans to send them to Cambridge, and describes meetings with Lyell, Owen, Grant, Bell, Broderip and other naturalists, publication advice, London versus Cambridge arrangements, and heavy specimen boxes. The letter is a composite sequence with later logistics; it asks Henslow to discuss publication and fossil-shell help but does not quote a surviving Henslow prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow [1 November 1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin sends a short follow-up about the Galapagos plant box and four heavier boxes, specifying their contents, safe storage and expected Cambridge arrival. He reports new naturalists willing to examine crustaceans, reptiles and shells and asks whether the plants arrived safely. This is a shipment/receipt inquiry, not evidence that a prior Henslow letter was read.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 18 May – 16 June 1832
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s first long voyage report explains the delayed writing, departure and seasickness, Tenerife quarantine, St Jago geology and collecting, Bahia/Rio travel, new marine and terrestrial animals, requests for useful books and a future box, shipboard relations, and the June 16 addendum with a postponed cargo and a Hymenophallus/Leiodes specimen. Its sections are one evolving outgoing report, with later dated additions rather than separate incoming prompts.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 [23 July –] 15 August [1832]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin describes specimens ready for dispatch from Rio, his dependence on Henslow’s Cambridge headquarters, and an apologetic account of sparse collections, then continues with South American travel, geological observations, insects and plans for future cargos. The date range and multiple continuation sections must remain distinct; a later shipment or book request is not itself an incoming Henslow letter.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 [c. 26 October –] 24 November [1832]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin sends a cargo with bird and animal skins, spirit specimens, seeds, granary sweepings and a large box of bones/geological material held at Armstrong's. He reports overland travel from the Rio Negro to Buenos Aires and Santa Fe, fossil-bone finds, asks for mineralogical guidance and books, and sets out the coming Tierra del Fuego/Chili route. The postscript about sea-weeds is a technical question to Henslow, not evidence of a prior Henslow prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 11 April 1833
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin reports the Tierra del Fuego cruise, its storms and non-fossiliferous geology, Fuegian observations, a Zoëa and anomalous decapod, Corallina work, Falklands fossils, and the coming South American route. He asks about useful books and a comet report and clarifies the geological context of a Megatherium. No Henslow text is quoted or uniquely answered within this letter.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 18 July 1833
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin explains that weather kept the Beagle at Maldonado, laments the absence of Henslow’s handwriting, describes four barrels of specimens and their handling, outlines the Rio Negro and Tierra del Fuego itinerary, and asks about a prior Tierra del Fuego geological collection and books. The forward-looking request for a letter and information does not identify an earlier surviving prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow [20–7] September 1833
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s brief September letter is an outgoing continuation about voyage logistics and correspondence; its short body is read in full, including its dated section and closing. It contains no Henslow answer or distinctive incoming quotation that can be assigned to a later target.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 12 November 1833
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin sends another cargo of skins, spirit bottles, seeds and granary sweepings, plus bones and geology via Armstrong, then narrates his dangerous overland route, fossil finds, requests a mineralogical book and advice, and comments on Tierra del Fuego. The closing asks whether sea-weeds should be sent in spirits after noting colour by Werner. The body diagram reference is an authorial comparison, and the referenced figure asset is not locally preserved for visual inspection.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: HTML references inline figure(s), but no preserved local asset was available for visual inspection.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 March 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin opens by thanking Henslow for the August 31 letter and for news that a prior cargo arrived safely. He discusses numbered Megatherium material, further cargos, plants and seeds, Patagonian and Tierra del Fuego geology, corallines and a second ostrich species, reports reading the Oxford Report, and describes unrest affecting shipment routes. The preserved diagram reference concerns an anomalous specimen; the local figure asset is unavailable, so only its textual context is assessed.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: HTML references inline figure(s), but no preserved local asset was available for visual inspection.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 24 July – 7 November 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin receives two delayed Henslow letters dated 12 December 1833 and 15 January 1834 and says they answer the packing and collection concerns he had wanted addressed. He reports notes, Planaria and Vaginulus, cargos and seed growth, fossil bones, Santa Cruz and Andes geology, corallines, a Cellaria and propagation observations, and further specimen logistics. This explicit receipt is a strong knowledge/response witness for the unlocated Henslow letters, but neither is one of the five assigned incoming contexts.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow 4 October 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s one-page notice says FitzRoy sent two casks, a box of bottles and a jar through Portsmouth, and promises to write again when well. It is a cargo notice with no substantive Henslow prompt or reply content; the supplied place line is separate from the dated letter body.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow 8 November 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s short outgoing notice says he is sending a cargo of specimens and asks Henslow to handle the consignments; the complete retained paragraphs and closing were checked. It contains no recoverable Henslow input.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To J. S. Henslow1 [10]–13 March 1835
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin gives a long account of Mendoza and the Cordilleras, revising geological views, describing strata, fossils, silicified trees, red snow and viviparous lizards, and listing seeds, dried plants, notebooks and other specimens sent with a cargo. The dated additions and altered plans remain separate sections; requests that Henslow examine or publish material are prospective and do not identify a prior Henslow text.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From J. S. Henslow 20 November 1831
incoming_reviews.summary: Henslow forwards plates for Lowe's paper through Jenyns, gives practical advice on surds, and offers extended counsel about tolerating rough shipmates and adapting to expedition hardships. He explicitly affirms Darwin’s fitness for the voyage; the plates and advice are a shipment and instruction, not a surviving response to the later target letters.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From J. S. Henslow 6 February 1832
incoming_reviews.summary: Henslow keeps Darwin’s requested first-Tuesday correspondence promise. He reports hearing of the departure through Yarrell and Captain King, Cambridge examination and political news, the Ramsay memorial, college appointments, and family matters, then revisits their Tierra del Fuego conversations and says he will continue writing. It supplies no distinctive natural-history prompt for the later Darwin targets.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From J. S. Henslow 15–21 January 1833
incoming_reviews.summary: Henslow’s two-stage January letter says he delayed writing to inspect Darwin’s arriving box, then explicitly answers two Darwin letters, beginning with the one dated 18 May. He reports receipt and condition of birds, quadrupeds, insects and lichens, asks about specimen 2231, urges duplicate memoranda and more shells, and says he forwards the Dictionary of Classical Antiquities. The full source also contains the inserted specimen diagram references; these are Henslow’s observations of received material, not Darwin voice.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: HTML references inline figure(s), but no preserved local asset was available for visual inspection.

incoming_reviews.title: From J. S. Henslow 31 August 1833
incoming_reviews.summary: Henslow acknowledges a Darwin cargo, notes spoiled spirit contents, and says he now has Darwin’s letter of the previous April. He reports the Megatherium's Geological Section exhibition and Clift's request to repair, figure and describe the fossils, explains storage of animals and plants, discusses the Ramsay memorial and comet, and encourages Darwin to continue. The explicit April reference and cargo handling make this a scoped response to Darwin’s preceding correspondence, while the full letter does not answer every intervening subject.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From J. S. Henslow 22 July 1834
incoming_reviews.summary: Henslow answers Darwin’s recent letter and cargo report: Armstrong has finally dispatched the safe cases, fossils were directed to Clift for repair and preparation, seeds may have spoiled, and Darwin should dry more plants and send minute material. He gives mineralogical advice about the goniometer and Phillips's book, discusses Darwin’s complaint about missing correspondence, Cambridge affairs and his own family. This is a direct but broad response to an unlocated recent Darwin letter/cargo, not a prompt for the assigned later outgoing letters.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

proposed_links.scope: DCP-LETT-196 P2-P3 answers the May 18 portion of the earlier Darwin letter and specimen cargo; it is not evidence for a complete answer to every section of DCP-LETT-171.

evidence.quote: The 1st date of your first letter is May 18. & this I received at Cambridge in June
I have just been putting bye the perishable articles in the way I said
I have determined not to send a box till we arrive at Monte Video.

proposed_links.scope: Henslow’s August 1833 letter explicitly identifies Darwin’s April letter and responds to its cargo and Megatherium contents; the relation is scoped to that acknowledged letter/cargo, not the full geological narrative.

evidence.quote: I am now in possession of your letter of last April
The fossil portions of the Megatherium turned out to be extremely interesting
I am convinced from talking to the finder

proposed_links.scope: Henslow answers Darwin’s recent letter and cargo report, with explicit receipt/dispatch details and advice matching Darwin’s consignments; source does not identify a complete one-to-one answer to every paragraph.

evidence.quote: It is now some months since I received your last letter
These were delayed at Dr Armstrongs
your account of the safe arrival of my second cargo

proposed_links.scope: Darwin explicitly says no letter has arrived in the final pre-return interval; no surviving Henslow context can be treated as read before this target.

evidence.quote: We have all been disappointed here in not finding even a single letter

proposed_links.scope: A home box with books and a letter from Henslow is reported as planned/expected, not received or read.

I cannot receive this before we reach Sydney

findings: DCP-LETT-150 is already adjudicated as replying to DCP-LETT-147; that completed relationship is preserved and not recounted as a new Beagle-voyage edge.
DCP-LETT-196, 213 and 249 provide the only distinctive surviving Henslow-to-Darwin response evidence in this scope; their dates and receipt stages are retained as XML ranges.

DCP-LETT-251 explicitly reports delayed receipt of two Henslow letters (12 December 1833 and 15 January 1834), but those physical letters are not among the five assigned contexts and are not substituted for them.
Darwin outgoing targets 274, 283, 295, 304, 311, 317 and 318 contain prospective questions, shipment notices or post-return planning; no additional surviving Henslow prompt is identified.
The old HTML pages for 196, 229 and 238 reference inline diagrams, but the corresponding local figure assets were not present; visual claims about those figures are held.
limitations: The packet plan is the navigation artifact; no separate Beagle-voyage packet or accepted ledger was present. Source HTML/XML hashes and paths were taken from the plan and checked against the files.
The plan’s target/context distinction excludes Henslow letters outside the five assigned contexts; unlocated or delayed Henslow letters are named only where Darwin/Henslow explicitly attest them.
Figure references in three preserved HTML pages lack local assets, so figure content was not inferred from alt text or adjacent prose.
